meta.title: Spot the move
meta.note: Move names and hint-ladder levels match spec/pedagogy-rules.md v1.0 of the Socratic AI Tutor (repo 03), 2026-10-25. All exchanges are fictional, constructed for training purposes, drawn from the transcript library.

items.source: Transcript T1 · strong session · guided practice
exchange: Tutor: New problem on the board: 2(x − 4) + 3 = 11. Before I say anything — Amara, what do you notice?
Amara: There's parentheses and a plus 3.

options.text: none of these — the tutor explained first

items.feedback: This is a probing question — ladder level 0. The tutor's first move hands the problem to the student ('what do you notice?'), which starts the diagnosis before any explanation. Contrast with the weak sessions: T5 opens with a 90-second monologue and never asks.

items.source: Transcript T1 · strong session · guided practice
exchange: Tutor: (says nothing for about four seconds)
Luis: …and the sign flips because we're subtracting minus 5.

options.text: none of these — the tutor left the student stuck

items.feedback: Wait time: 3–5 seconds of silence after a question or a student's half-answer. The tutor resists confirming, prompting, or rephrasing the question into a giveaway — and the student finishes the reasoning himself. In T6, by contrast, the tutor talks over the student's 'But—' within one second.

items.source: Transcript T2 · strong session · third failure on the same step
exchange: Mei: Mine keeps coming out wrong. (third failed attempt at the −3 move) I keep getting positive 3. This is stupid.

Tutor: It's not stupid — that −3 is genuinely the sneakiest part of this problem type, and you're in good company. New plan: watch me do one like it, all the way through, and your only job is to catch the moment the −3 gets handled.
items.feedback: Worked example after repeated failure — the ladder's L4. After ~three failures on the same step, more hints stop helping; the tutor resets the emotion first ('not stupid … good company'), works a SIMILAR problem fully (never the student's own), narrates the exact step that keeps failing, then hands the original back. T2 shows the hand-back; without it, worked examples entertain instead of transfer.

items.source: Transcript T3 · mixed session · check that failed
exchange: Tutor: Recompute the check with x = 4: left is 3(4) + 7 = 19. Right is 2(4) + 19…

options.text: none of these — the tutor did the arithmetic for the student

items.feedback: None of the seven moves: the tutor computed FOR the student ('left is 3(4) + 7 = 19') instead of asking her to compute. It kept the session moving and the thinking partly alive — hence 'partly' — but Jayla's role shrank to reading numbers. The stronger line: 'Compute both sides with x = 4 — what do you get?'

items.source: Transcript T4 · mixed session · two correct answers
exchange: Priya: Subtract 5 both sides: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.
Tutor: Good job! … Camila: x = 5! — Tutor: Nice work!

options.text: none of these — generic praise, not specific feedback

items.feedback: Not specific feedback — it's generic praise, and the distinction matters: specific feedback names WHAT in the work was right ('you subtracted before dividing, so the coefficient stayed clean'), which the student can then repeat. 'Good job' could be said to any student for anything — so it teaches nothing and quietly certifies that approval, not understanding, is the currency.

items.source: Transcript T5 · weak session · the opening
exchange: Tutor: …today we're doing equations with parentheses, which look scary but are actually the easiest kind once you see the trick, because all you do is distribute first, and distributing just means multiplying the outside number by everything inside… (continues, uninterrupted, for about 90 seconds)

options.text: none of these — a solution monologue with no question

items.feedback: None of the moves: this is over-explaining — every fact correct, every student passive. Ladder level 0 exists precisely for the start of a problem: 'What have you tried?' or 'What do you notice?' The attempt is the diagnosis. In T5 the students produce nothing for nine minutes; in T1 the same content starts with a student noticing.

items.source: Transcript T5 · weak session · the one real error
exchange: Tutor: You're close, but no — when you distribute, the 2 has to multiply both things inside, so it's 2x − 8, not 2x − 4. Let me write it: 2 times −4 is −8. Okay?

options.text: none of these — the tutor named and corrected the error

items.feedback: This is correcting the error outright — the tutor names the misconception, performs the fix, and ends with 'Okay?' (approval-seeking). The rule it breaks: expose, don't correct. 'What did the 2 multiply?' points the student at the exact spot and lets HER find −8. Self-found fixes stick; received fixes evaporate by Thursday.

items.source: Transcript T6 · weak session · Aaliyah's sign error
exchange: Aaliyah: For 7x − 2 = 4x + 10, I got x = 2… but the check doesn't work?
Tutor: Let me look — oh, you did 7x − 4x and then moved the 2 but added it: 3x + 2 = 10, that's your bug, it should be minus 2 both sides, so 3x = 12, x = 4. Check it now.

options.text: none of these — diagnosed, corrected, and solved by the tutor

items.feedback: Three violations in six seconds: the error is named ('that's your bug'), the fix is executed by the tutor, and the student's role is reduced to re-checking someone else's solution. This is the answer-for-the-student failure mode. The ladder's L1–L2 exist for exactly this moment: 'When you moved the −2, what did you do to both sides?' — Aaliyah would have met the subtraction meaning of 'moving terms' instead of collecting another patched rule.

items.source: Transcript T2 · strong session · after Mei's breakthrough
exchange: Tutor: You did the whole ladder yourself. Why subtract the 5 and not add it?
items.feedback: Confirm and ask why: brief confirmation ('you did the whole ladder yourself') followed by ONE why-question. The why at the moment of success is where understanding consolidates — and then the tutor moves on, rather than interrogating a right answer. The very next line of T2 is the other half of the chain: 'One more, same shape…' — the offer of a similar problem.

items.source: Transcript T1 · strong session · independent try
exchange: Tutor: Same shape, new numbers: 3(x + 2) − 5 = 16. Solo, four minutes — I'm not talking. If you finish, check by substituting.
items.feedback: Offer a similar problem after a solved one — same structure, one small variation — as a quiet test of whether the method (not just this answer) transferred. 'I'm not talking' is the point: the offer keeps ownership with the student, and the silence is what makes the transfer evidence real. T6's 'speed round' is the corrupted version: racing, not transferring.
